steps: Step 1, Say what a shadow is. Hold a book between a torch and a wall. Light travels in straight lines from the torch, but the book is in the way, so a dark shape appears on the wall behind it. Say: 'The book blocks the light, so it makes a shadow.'

Step 2, Set up a safe test. Darken the room a little and shine a torch on a wall from 30 cm away. Safety: never look straight at the sun and never shine a torch into anyone's eyes. Collect six things: clear plastic cup, tracing paper, cardboard, foil, a book and a thin white tissue.

Step 3, Hold each object between the torch and the wall and look at the shadow. The clear cup lets almost all light through, so there is hardly any shadow. Tracing paper and tissue let some light through, so the shadow is pale. Cardboard, foil and the book let none through, so the shadow is dark.

Step 4, Name three groups and sort your six things. Transparent: lets light through (clear cup). Translucent: lets some light through (tracing paper, tissue). Opaque: lets no light through (cardboard, foil, book). Draw three boxes and write each object in the right box.

Step 5, Find where the shadow falls. Stand a small toy 20 cm in front of the torch. The shadow lands on the far side of the toy, away from the light. Move the toy closer to the torch and the shadow grows bigger; move it away and the shadow gets smaller.

Step 6, Your turn: you want the darkest possible shadow. Choose between a clear glass, a sheet of tracing paper and a piece of thick card, then say why. Answer: choose the thick card, because it is opaque and lets no light through, so its shadow is darkest.

Step 1, Plan breakfast. A healthy start has something from each group: bread or oats for energy, milk or egg to help you grow, and a piece of fruit such as a banana to keep you well. Write: 'Breakfast, 7:00, egg, bread, fruit and a glass of water.'

Step 2, Plan lunch and snacks. Lunch at 12:30 could be rice, chicken or beans, and vegetables such as carrot and cucumber. A snack at 10:00 could be an apple or yoghurt. Keep sweets and fizzy drinks for rare treats, and drink water through the day, about six to eight cups.

Step 3, Plan play and exercise. Children need about 60 minutes of active play every day. Write times for it: running at break, riding a bike at 4:00, and a game in the garden. Play makes your heart, bones and muscles strong, and it helps you feel happy.

Step 4, Plan sleep and cleanliness. Children aged six to eight need about 9 to 11 hours of sleep. If you wake at 6:30, bedtime should be about 8:30. Wash your hands before meals and after the toilet, and brush your teeth in the morning and at night.

Step 5, Put the day in a table with four columns: Time, What I do, Healthy part, Why it helps. Example row: 'Bedtime 8:30, read then sleep, sleep, my body rests and grows'. Fill in at least six rows from morning to night.

Step 6, Your turn: plan a healthy afternoon from 3:00 to bedtime with one snack, one kind of play and a bedtime. Model answer: 3:00 apple and water, 4:00 football outside for one hour, 6:00 dinner with vegetables, 8:00 wash and brush teeth, 8:30 sleep.

Step 1, Name the parts and their jobs. Roots hold the plant in the soil and take in water. The stem holds the plant up and carries water to the leaves. Leaves use sunlight to make food. The flower makes seeds, and the fruit protects them. Draw a bean plant and label these five parts.

Step 2, Watch a seed start growing. Put a bean seed on damp cotton wool in a clear cup near a window. After about 3 to 5 days the root comes out first, then the shoot. Safety: wash your hands afterwards and never eat seeds that have been in soil or cotton.

Step 3, Test what a root does. Stand a white flower or a celery stick in water with a little red food dye. After a day the colour climbs the stem, which shows that stems carry water up. Write: 'Water goes from the roots, up the stem, to the leaves.'

Step 4, Learn how seeds spread, because a seed that falls under its parent has little room, light or water. Wind carries light seeds such as dandelion. Water carries a coconut across the sea. Animals carry sticky burrs on fur, or eat berries and drop the seeds far away.

Step 5, Match plants to ways of spreading. Dandelion has fluffy parachutes, so wind. Coconut floats, so water. Burdock has hooks, so animals' fur. Pea pods dry and pop open, so the seeds are thrown out. Draw one arrow from each seed to its way of travelling.
Step 6, Your turn: a plant has small, light seeds with thin wings. How are they spread, and which part takes in water? Answer: the wings let the wind carry them away; the roots take in water.

Step 1, Learn the idea of adaptation. An adaptation is a body feature that helps an animal live well in its habitat. A habitat is the place where an animal lives. Link each feature to a need such as finding food, getting water, staying cool or escaping enemies.

Step 2, Study a desert animal. A camel has wide, flat feet that do not sink in sand, long eyelashes and closable nostrils to keep sand out, and a hump that stores fat as food for long journeys. A fennec fox has huge ears that lose heat and keep it cool.

Step 3, Study more desert features. Many lizards are sand-coloured, so they are hard to see. Desert rodents sleep in cool burrows by day and come out at night. These features help the animals find food and water, and stay safe from the hot sun.

Step 4, Study sea animals. A fish has a smooth, streamlined body, fins to steer and a tail to push, and gills to take oxygen from water. A dolphin is a mammal, so it breathes air through a blowhole on top of its head and comes up to breathe.

Step 5, Make a table with three columns: Animal, Feature, Why it helps. Row 1: camel, wide feet, walks on sand without sinking. Row 2: fish, gills, breathes underwater. Row 3: fennec fox, big ears, loses body heat. Add a fourth row of your own.

Step 6, Your turn: a shark has a streamlined body and fins, and a lizard has sandy skin. Link each to a habitat. Answer: the shark's smooth body and fins help it swim fast in the sea; the lizard's sandy colour hides it in the desert.

Step 1, Group food into nutrients. Carbohydrates, such as rice and bread, give energy. Proteins, such as egg, fish and beans, help the body grow and repair. Fats, such as butter and nuts, store energy. Vitamins and minerals, found in fruit and vegetables, keep us healthy. Water is needed too.

Step 2, Sort a real lunch: rice (carbohydrate), grilled fish (protein), salad (vitamins and minerals), olive oil (fat) and a glass of water. Draw a plate and write the nutrient beside each food. A balanced meal has some of each group, not only one.

Step 3, Follow the first part of the journey. Food enters the mouth, where teeth cut and grind it and saliva makes it soft and wet. Then you swallow, and the food slides down the food pipe, called the oesophagus, which squeezes it along.

Step 4, Follow the middle of the journey. In the stomach the food is churned with juices for a few hours until it is a thick liquid. Then it moves to the small intestine, a long coiled tube, where the useful nutrients pass into the blood.

Step 5, Finish the journey. What cannot be used, such as fibre, goes to the large intestine, where water is taken back into the body. The rest leaves the body as waste. Draw the path as arrows: mouth, food pipe, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, out.

Step 6, Your turn: name the nutrient group of egg, bread and orange, and say where nutrients enter the blood. Answer: egg is protein, bread is carbohydrate, orange gives vitamins; nutrients enter the blood in the small intestine.

Step 1, Explain how a shadow forms. Light from a source, such as the sun, travels in straight lines. When an opaque object blocks the rays, no light reaches the space behind it, and that dark space is the shadow. The shadow is always on the side opposite the light.

Step 2, Measure a real shadow. Stand a 1 metre stick upright in sunlight. Measure the shadow at 9:00, 12:00 and 3:00 with a ruler. Safety: never look at the sun, and wear a hat. A typical result is long in the morning, shortest at noon and long again in the afternoon.

Step 3, Explain the change. In the morning and evening the sun is low in the sky, so the shadow is long. At noon the sun is highest, so the shadow is shortest. For a 1 m stick, a sun 30 degrees high gives a shadow of about 1.7 m, and 60 degrees gives about 0.6 m.

Step 4, Explain the direction. The sun is in the east in the morning, so shadows point west. In the afternoon the sun is in the west, so shadows point east. The shadow always points away from the sun and swings round as the sun moves across the sky.

Step 5, Test it indoors with a torch and a pencil. Hold the torch low and close to the table and the pencil's shadow is long. Raise the torch high above the pencil and the shadow becomes short. Measure both shadows and record them in a table.

Step 6, Your turn: at 8:00 a tree's shadow is 6 m long, and at 12:00 it is 1 m. Which time has the higher sun and which way does the 8:00 shadow point? Answer: noon has the higher sun; the morning shadow points west.

Step 1, Describe pushes and pulls. A force is a push or a pull. Opening a door by its handle is a pull, and pressing a doorbell is a push. A force can start something moving, stop it, speed it up, slow it down, change its direction or change its shape.

Step 2, Measure a pull. Use a spring balance to pull a toy box across the floor. Force is measured in newtons (N). Say the balance reads 4 N: that is the pull needed to keep it moving. Safety: keep fingers away from the spring and the box.

Step 3, Meet friction. Friction is a force that acts when two surfaces rub, and it tries to stop movement. Pull the same box across tiles and then a carpet. A typical reading is 3 N on tiles and 8 N on carpet, because rougher surfaces have more friction.

Step 4, Feel friction at work. Rub your hands together quickly: they get warm because friction changes movement into heat. Friction is useful in shoe soles and brakes, which grip, but not in machine parts, so we use oil to reduce it.

Step 5, Test a ramp. Let a toy car roll down a ramp onto a smooth board, then onto a towel. On the board it travels, for example, 120 cm, and on the towel only 40 cm, because the towel has more friction. Write which surface slows the car most.
Step 6, Your turn: a box needs 3 N on tiles and 8 N on carpet. Which surface has more friction, and how many more newtons? Answer: carpet has more friction, by 8 - 3 = 5 N.

Step 1, Link the sun to day and night. The sun seems to rise in the east in the morning and set in the west in the evening. This is because the Earth spins once every 24 hours. The side facing the sun has day, and the side facing away has night.

Step 2, Link the sun to weather. The sun warms the land and sea. Warm water rises as vapour, cools into clouds, and may fall as rain. Record the weather for five days with symbols for sunny, cloudy and rainy, and a thermometer reading each noon.

Step 3, Observe the moon. The moon does not make its own light; it reflects light from the sun. It seems to change shape in a cycle of about 29 days: new moon, crescent, half, full, and back again. Draw the moon each night for a week. Safety: do this with an adult.

Step 4, Explain the seasons. The Earth goes round the sun once a year, and it is tilted. So for part of the year each place has longer days and more direct sunlight, which brings summer. In the UAE summer afternoons can be above 40 degrees Celsius, and winter days are about 25.

Step 5, Show a pattern chart with columns for Month, Daylight, Weather and What people wear. In summer: long days, hot and dry, light clothes. In winter: shorter days, cooler, a jumper in the evening. Fill in four rows and link each row to the sun's position.

Step 6, Your turn: why is the night sky different on a new moon and a full moon? Answer: on a full moon we see the whole sunlit face of the moon, on a new moon we see almost none of it, because of where the moon is in its journey round the Earth.

Step 1, Define adaptation in plants. An adaptation is a feature that helps a plant survive in its habitat. Plants cannot move away, so their roots, stems and leaves must suit the place: little water in a desert, lots of water in a pond, and freezing cold on a mountain.

Step 2, Study a desert plant. A cactus has a thick, fleshy stem that stores water. Its leaves are narrow spines, which lose very little water and keep animals away. Its roots spread wide just under the sand to catch rare rain. Its waxy skin seals water in.

Step 3, Study a water plant. A water lily has leaves that float flat on top, to catch sunlight. Its stems have air spaces so that it floats and the roots in the mud can get oxygen. The stems are soft and bendy, so they move with the water without snapping.

Step 4, Study a cold-habitat plant. A pine tree has narrow needle leaves with a waxy coat, which lose little water when the ground is frozen. Its cone shape and bending branches let snow slide off, so branches do not break under the weight.

Step 5, Build a comparison table with columns Habitat, Plant, Feature, Job. Row 1: desert, cactus, thick stem, stores water. Row 2: pond, water lily, air spaces, floats. Row 3: cold mountain, pine, sloping branches, sheds snow. Add a fourth row, a date palm with deep roots that reach water.

Step 6, Your turn: a plant has thin, waxy leaves, spines and a swollen stem. Which habitat suits it, and why? Answer: a desert, because the swollen stem stores water, spines and waxy skin reduce water loss.

Step 1, Learn the roles. A food chain shows who eats whom. It starts with a producer, a green plant that makes its own food from sunlight. A consumer eats other living things. Herbivores eat plants, and carnivores eat animals. Arrows point to the eater, showing the direction energy moves.

Step 2, Build a land chain: grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, eagle. Grass is the producer. The grasshopper is the first consumer. The frog and snake are middle consumers, and the eagle is at the top. Write it with arrows: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle.

Step 3, Build a sea chain: tiny floating plants (plankton) → small fish → tuna → shark. The producer is the plankton, which makes food in sunlight near the surface. The shark has no natural enemies in this chain. Draw the arrows pointing to the eater each time.

Step 4, Explain energy loss. Each animal uses most of the energy it eats for moving and keeping warm. Only about a tenth passes on. If grass holds 10,000 units, the grasshopper gets about 1,000, the frog about 100 and the snake about 10. So chains are short.

Step 5, Explain adaptation within a chain. An eagle has sharp eyes, hooked beak and strong claws for catching prey. A frog has a long sticky tongue for insects. A grasshopper is green and hides in grass. Each feature helps it eat or avoid being eaten.

Step 6, Your turn: build a three-link desert chain from seeds, a desert mouse and a fox, and say which energy amount the fox gets if seeds hold 1,000 units. Answer: seeds → mouse → fox; the mouse gets about 100 and the fox about 10 units.

Step 1, Follow digestion from the mouth. Digestion breaks food into tiny pieces that the blood can carry. In the mouth, teeth chew and saliva starts to digest starch. Chew a plain cracker for a minute: it begins to taste a little sweet. Do this only with clean food at home.

Step 2, Follow food onward. The food pipe moves it to the stomach, where muscles churn it with acid and juices. Next, the small intestine finishes digestion and moves nutrients into the blood. The large intestine takes back water, and waste leaves the body.

Step 3, Learn tooth types. An adult has 32 teeth: 8 incisors for cutting, 4 canines for tearing, 8 premolars and 12 molars for grinding. Check: 8 + 4 + 8 + 12 = 32. Young children have 20 milk teeth, which later fall out and are replaced.

Step 4, Know the parts of a tooth. The hard white outside is enamel, which protects the tooth. Under it is softer dentine, and inside is the pulp, with nerves and blood. Bacteria in plaque turn sugar into acid, and the acid wears away enamel, causing holes called cavities.

Step 5, Plan tooth care. Brush for two minutes, twice a day, with fluoride toothpaste, and clean between teeth. Eat fewer sweets and sugary drinks, and visit a dentist about every six months. Make a chart and tick each day you brush morning and night.

Step 6, Your turn: which teeth cut an apple, and where does digestion of starch begin? Answer: the incisors cut the apple; digestion of starch begins in the mouth, where saliva starts to break it down.

Step 1, Group animals by diet. Herbivores eat plants (goat, camel), carnivores eat other animals (lion, falcon) and omnivores eat both (bear, human). Check the teeth: flat grinding molars suit plants, and sharp canines suit meat. Sort eight animals into three columns.

Step 2, Group animals by habitat. Land habitats include desert, forest and grassland. Water habitats include rivers, ponds and the sea. Some animals use both, such as frogs. Place each of your eight animals in a habitat and write one feature that fits it, such as a camel's wide feet.

Step 3, Learn complete life cycles. A butterfly goes through egg, larva (caterpillar), pupa and adult: four stages. Each stage looks very different. A frog goes through egg, tadpole, froglet and adult, and a tadpole lives in water and breathes with gills.

Step 4, Learn simpler life cycles. A grasshopper has egg, nymph and adult: three stages, and a nymph looks like a small adult without wings. Birds and reptiles lay eggs, while most mammals, such as cats and humans, give birth to live young and feed them milk.

Step 5, Put it in a table with columns Animal, Diet, Habitat, Life cycle. Example row: butterfly, herbivore (nectar), garden, egg → larva → pupa → adult. Another: lion, carnivore, grassland, born live and fed with milk. Complete six rows.
Step 6, Your turn: classify a frog by diet, habitat and life cycle. Answer: a carnivore, because it eats insects; it lives in water and on land; its life cycle is egg, tadpole, froglet and adult.

Step 1, Describe the skeletal system. An adult skeleton has 206 bones. It supports the body, protects organs (the skull protects the brain and the ribs protect the heart and lungs) and gives muscles something to pull on. Joints, such as the knee and elbow, let bones move.

Step 2, Describe the muscular system. Muscles pull but cannot push, so they work in pairs. When the biceps in your upper arm contracts, your elbow bends; when the triceps contracts, it straightens. Make a fist, bend your arm and feel the biceps harden.

Step 3, Describe the respiratory system. Air goes in through the nose, down the windpipe, into two bronchi and then the lungs, ending in tiny air sacs called alveoli. There oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out. At rest a child breathes about 20 times a minute.

Step 4, Describe the circulatory system. The heart pumps blood around the body in blood vessels. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, and veins bring it back. Blood carries oxygen and nutrients to every cell. Find your pulse at your wrist: about 80 beats a minute is usual at rest.

Step 5, Calculate heart work. At 75 beats a minute the heart beats 75 x 60 x 24 = 108,000 times a day. Then try exercise: jog on the spot for one minute and count the pulse again. Safety: stop if you feel dizzy or breathless, and sit down.

Step 6, Your turn: name the system that has a biceps and triceps, and one that has alveoli. Then state the heart beats in 2 hours at 75 per minute. Answer: muscular; respiratory; 75 x 120 = 9,000 beats.

Step 1, Separate reversible from irreversible changes. In a reversible change the material can go back to how it was, such as ice melting to water and freezing again. In an irreversible change a new material forms and cannot go back, such as burning paper, baking dough or rusting.

Step 2, Test a reversible change. Put one ice cube in a cup, let it melt and note that it becomes water. Place that water in the freezer and it freezes again. Write 'melting and freezing are reversible: no new substance is made'.

Step 3, Test an irreversible change, carefully. Put 2 spoons of bicarbonate of soda in a tray and add 50 mL of vinegar. It fizzes and makes a gas, so a new substance has formed. Safety: wear goggles, do it with an adult, and never taste or smell closely.

Step 4, Tell mixtures from solutions. Sand and water make a mixture: the grains stay separate and can be filtered out. Salt in water makes a solution: the salt dissolves and seems to vanish, but it is still there. Stir 5 g of salt into 100 mL of water until clear.

Step 5, Get the dissolved material back. Pour the salt solution into a shallow dish and leave it in the sun for a day or two, or heat it only with an adult's help. The water evaporates and white salt crystals stay behind. Dissolving is therefore reversible, and the mass is the same: 10 g sugar and 100 g water give a 110 g solution.

Step 6, Your turn: classify these as reversible or irreversible, and say whether sand in water is a mixture or a solution. Egg frying, ice melting, wood burning. Answer: egg frying irreversible, ice melting reversible, wood burning irreversible; sand in water is a mixture.

Step 1, Say where food comes from. Plants give us cereals (wheat, rice), pulses, fruits, vegetables and oils. Animals give us milk, eggs, meat and fish. Honey comes from bees. Sort twelve foods from your kitchen into plant source, animal source or both, such as a cake made with flour, eggs and milk.

Step 2, Group the nutrients. Carbohydrates give energy, proteins build and repair the body, fats give stored energy, vitamins and minerals protect the body and help it work, fibre helps digestion, and water carries things around the body. Pair each nutrient with two foods, such as rice and potato for carbohydrates.

Step 3, Prepare the starch test. Starch turns iodine solution from brown-orange to blue-black. Safety: iodine stains skin and clothes and is harmful if swallowed, so wear goggles and gloves, use a few drops, never taste anything in the test, and wash hands afterwards. Do this with a teacher or adult.

Step 4, Run the test. Place a small piece of each food on a white plate: potato, bread, apple and boiled egg white. Add 2 drops of dilute iodine to each. Potato and bread turn blue-black, so they contain starch. Apple shows almost no change, and egg white stays brown.

Step 5, Record the result in a table with columns Food, Colour after iodine, Starch present?. Potato: blue-black, yes. Bread: blue-black, yes. Apple: brown, no (or very little). Egg white: brown, no. Write a conclusion: 'Foods that turned blue-black contain starch, a carbohydrate.'
Step 6, Your turn: a food sample turns blue-black with iodine. Which nutrient is present, and which group does it belong to? Answer: starch is present; it is a carbohydrate, which gives energy.

Step 1, Meet natural fibres. Cotton comes from the fluffy boll around the seeds of the cotton plant, wool comes from sheep's fur, silk comes from the cocoon of the silkworm and jute comes from plant stems. Synthetic fibres, such as nylon and polyester, are made in factories from chemicals.

Step 2, Follow cotton to cloth. Cotton is picked, the seeds are removed (ginning), the fibres are spun into yarn, and the yarn is woven or knitted into fabric. Draw four boxes in order: picking, ginning, spinning, weaving, and write one sentence under each.

Step 3, Test absorbency. Cut 10 cm squares of cotton, polyester and nylon. Drop 5 mL of water on each with a dropper and time how long it takes to soak in. Cotton soaks it quickly, so it is absorbent and good for towels; polyester repels it, so it suits raincoats. Safety: do not burn fabrics.

Step 4, Sort materials by properties: hard or soft, rough or smooth, transparent or opaque, strong or weak, and whether they float or sink. Steel is hard and strong; glass is hard and transparent; rubber is flexible; wood floats; iron sinks. Make a table of eight materials.

Step 5, Link properties to uses. Copper conducts electricity, so it is used in wires. Plastic does not conduct, so it covers the wires. Steel is strong, so it is used in bridges. Glass is transparent, so it is used in windows. Write: 'The material is chosen because it is ...'.

Step 6, Your turn: choose a fabric for a rain jacket and a towel, and give a property for each. Answer: rain jacket, polyester or nylon, because it is waterproof; towel, cotton, because it is absorbent.

Step 1, Define terms. A habitat is the natural home of a living thing, such as a pond, desert or forest. An adaptation is a feature of the body or behaviour that helps it live there. Habitats can be on land (terrestrial) or in water (aquatic).

Step 2, Name the parts of a flowering plant. Roots anchor and absorb water. The stem supports and carries water and food. Leaves make food by photosynthesis. Flowers make seeds. Label a drawing of a mustard plant with these four parts and one job for each.

Step 3, Name the parts of an animal. An insect such as an ant has a head, a thorax with 6 legs and an abdomen, so 3 body parts. A fish has head, trunk and tail with fins. A bird has a beak, wings, feathers and two legs. Draw an ant and label each part.

Step 4, Link adaptation to parts. A hawk has a hooked beak for tearing meat. A duck has a flat beak and webbed feet for swimming and feeding in water. A camel has wide feet. A water lily has floating leaves. Write the part, the habitat and the benefit.

Step 5, Compare two habitats in a table with columns Habitat, Plant, Animal, Adaptation. Desert: cactus, camel, stores water. Pond: water lily, fish, floats and swims. Add a third row for a forest: tall tree, monkey, climbing with a gripping tail or hands.

Step 6, Your turn: a frog is found near a pond and has webbed feet and long back legs. State its habitat and one adaptation with its use. Answer: an aquatic and land habitat near water; webbed feet help it swim, and long back legs help it jump.

Step 1, Measure length. The metre is the standard unit: 1 m = 100 cm = 1000 mm. Measure your desk edge with a ruler, placing the zero mark at the start and reading from directly above to avoid error. Say the length in two units: for 1.35 m, that is 135 cm, or 1350 mm.

Step 2, Measure a curved line. A ruler cannot bend, so lay a thread along the curve, mark both ends on the thread, straighten it and measure it. If the thread reads 24.5 cm, the curve is 24.5 cm long. Practise on the outline of a leaf.

Step 3, Measure time. Use a stopwatch for short times: seconds (s) and minutes (1 min = 60 s). Time how long a marble rolls down a ramp three times, such as 2.1 s, 2.0 s and 2.2 s, and find the average: (2.1 + 2.0 + 2.2) / 3 = 2.1 s.

Step 4, Name types of motion. Straight-line motion is a car on a straight road. Circular motion is a stone whirling on a string. Rotational motion is a spinning top. Periodic or back-and-forth motion is a swing or a pendulum, which repeats the same path.

Step 5, Measure a pendulum. Time 20 swings of a pendulum; say it takes 36 s. One swing takes 36 / 20 = 1.8 s, called the time period. Also, a runner who goes 100 m in 20 s has speed 100 / 20 = 5 m/s. Safety: keep clear of swinging weights.
Step 6, Your turn: a cyclist rides 60 m in 12 s, and a pendulum makes 10 swings in 15 s. Find the speed and the time period. Answer: speed 60 / 12 = 5 m/s; time period 15 / 10 = 1.5 s.

Step 1, Show that light travels in straight lines. Take three cards with a hole in the middle. Line them up so that you can see a torch through all three holes. Move the middle card slightly sideways and the light is blocked. Conclusion: light travels in a straight line.

Step 2, Keep safe. Use a torch or lamp, never a naked flame, and never look at the sun or shine light into eyes. Mirrors have sharp edges, so handle them with care and place them on a table. Do not reflect sunlight into anyone's face.

Step 3, Observe reflection in a plane mirror. Light bounces off a mirror. Shine a torch beam at a mirror at an angle: the angle in, called the angle of incidence, equals the angle out, called the angle of reflection. If it enters at 40 degrees, it leaves at 40 degrees.

Step 4, Study the image. Stand 2 m in front of a plane mirror. Your image appears 2 m behind it, so you are 4 m from your image. It is the same size as you, and sideways reversed: raise your right hand and the image seems to raise its left.

Step 5, Use two mirrors to make a periscope. Place the mirrors at 45 degrees, one at the top and one at the bottom of a cardboard tube. Light from an object hits the top mirror, bounces down to the lower mirror and into your eye, so you can see over a wall.

Step 6, Your turn: a beam hits a mirror at 25 degrees, and you stand 3 m from the mirror. State the reflection angle and the distance to your image. Answer: reflection angle 25 degrees; the image is 3 m behind the mirror, so 6 m from you.

Step 1, Learn about indicators. Acids taste sour (lemon, vinegar) and bases feel slippery (soap). Indicators change colour to tell them apart. Litmus turns blue paper red in acid and red paper blue in a base. Safety: never taste chemicals, wear goggles and use only dilute household samples.

Step 2, Make a red cabbage indicator. Boil chopped red cabbage in water with an adult, and let the purple juice cool. Add a few drops to lemon juice: it goes pink-red. Add to baking soda solution: it goes blue-green. Water stays purple, so it is neutral.

Step 3, Read the pH scale. pH runs from 0 to 14. Below 7 is acidic (lemon juice about 2, vinegar about 3). pH 7 is neutral (pure water). Above 7 is basic (baking soda solution about 9, soapy water about 10). Place five liquids on a number line.

Step 4, Describe neutralisation. When an acid and a base react, they cancel each other's effects, making a salt and water. Hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide gives sodium chloride + water. Check atoms: HCl + NaOH gives NaCl + H2O, with 1 Na, 1 Cl, 2 H and 1 O on both sides.

Step 5, Use neutralisation in life. An antacid tablet, which is a weak base, neutralises extra stomach acid in indigestion. Farmers add lime to soil that is too acidic. Toothpaste is slightly basic, so it helps to neutralise the acid made by mouth bacteria.

Step 6, Your turn: a liquid turns red litmus blue and has pH 10. State if it is an acid or base, and what to add to neutralise it. Answer: it is a base; add a little dilute acid, such as vinegar, to neutralise it.

Step 1, Separate weather from climate. Weather is the condition of the air at a place and time, such as hot, windy or rainy today. Climate is the average weather over many years, usually 30. Say: 'It rained today' is weather; 'the desert is dry' is climate.

Step 2, Use the instruments. A thermometer measures temperature in degrees Celsius, a rain gauge measures rainfall in millimetres, an anemometer measures wind speed and a barometer measures air pressure. Safety: never use a thermometer to stir, and tell an adult if a thermometer breaks.

Step 3, Read a week of data. Maximum temperatures in a city were 31, 33, 35, 36, 34, 32 and 33 degrees Celsius. The highest is 36, the lowest is 31, so the range is 5. The mean is (31 + 33 + 35 + 36 + 34 + 32 + 33) / 7 = 234 / 7, about 33.4.

Step 4, Draw a bar chart of monthly rainfall. Suppose January 12 mm, February 18 mm, March 15 mm and the rest under 3 mm. The wettest months are the first three, and the total for the three is 45 mm. This tells you the climate is dry with a short wet season.

Step 5, Relate climate to living things. In dry climates, plants such as cacti store water and animals are active at night. In a rainforest, which gets over 2000 mm of rain a year, plants grow tall with large leaves. In polar climates, animals have thick fur or fat.

Step 6, Your turn: daily maximums are 28, 30, 29, 31 and 27. Find the range and mean, then name one adaptation for a very dry climate. Answer: range 31 - 27 = 4; mean 145 / 5 = 29; a cactus stores water in its stem.

Step 1, Define speed. Speed = distance / time. A walker who covers 6 m in 3 s has speed 6 / 3 = 2 m/s. On a distance-time graph, time goes on the horizontal axis and distance on the vertical axis, so a steeper line means a faster object.

Step 2, Read a graph. A runner is at 0 m at 0 s, 20 m at 4 s, still at 20 m at 6 s, and 60 m at 10 s. From 0 to 4 s the speed is 20 / 4 = 5 m/s. From 4 to 6 s the line is flat, so the runner is at rest. From 6 to 10 s the speed is 40 / 4 = 10 m/s.

Step 3, Find average speed over the whole run: total distance 60 m over total time 10 s is 6 m/s. Note that the average is not the same as the speed in any one part. Plot the points on graph paper, join them with a ruler and label the axes with units.

Step 4, Build a simple circuit. Use a cell, a bulb, a switch and wires. Close the switch and the bulb lights, because the circuit is a complete loop. Open the switch and the loop is broken, so the bulb goes out. Safety: use only small cells, never mains sockets, and do not short the cell with a wire.

Step 5, Draw circuit symbols: cell, bulb, switch, wire and ammeter. Current is measured in amperes (A). In a series circuit with two bulbs, the same current flows through both, say 0.3 A, and the bulbs are dimmer. In a parallel circuit each bulb has its own path.

Step 6, Your turn: a cyclist goes 30 m in 10 s, rests for 5 s, then goes 30 m more in 5 s. Find the speed in each moving part and the average over 20 s. Answer: 3 m/s and 6 m/s; average 60 / 20 = 3 m/s.

Step 1, Describe respiration. Living things release energy from food in a process called respiration, and it occurs in every cell. In word form: glucose + oxygen gives carbon dioxide + water + energy. In symbols: C6H12O6 + 6O2 gives 6CO2 + 6H2O. Count carbon, hydrogen and oxygen to check.

Step 2, Describe breathing in animals. Humans take in air through the nose and trachea to the lungs. Fish pass water over gills, insects breathe through tiny holes called spiracles, and earthworms take in oxygen through their moist skin. All of them move oxygen in and carbon dioxide out.

Step 3, Describe breathing in plants. Leaves have tiny pores called stomata, mostly underneath. They let oxygen and carbon dioxide move in and out, and water vapour leave. Roots take in oxygen from air spaces in the soil, which is why waterlogged soil can harm plants.

Step 4, Describe transport in plants. Xylem tubes carry water and minerals up from the roots to the leaves. Phloem tubes carry food made in the leaves to all other parts. Place a celery stalk in water with red food dye, and after several hours slice it to see coloured dots, which show the xylem.

Step 5, Describe transport in humans. The heart pumps blood through arteries, veins and capillaries. Red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs to the cells, and plasma carries food and waste. Plants also move pollen to make seeds, a reproduction link to transport. Safety: use a knife only with adult help.

Step 6, Your turn: name the plant tube that carries water up, and say what gas fish take in through gills. Then check that 6CO2 has 6 carbon atoms. Answer: xylem; oxygen dissolved in water; 6 x 1 = 6 carbon atoms, matching C6H12O6.

Step 1, Describe cell structure. A cell is the basic unit of life. Every cell has a membrane, which controls what goes in and out, cytoplasm, where reactions happen, and a nucleus, which holds the instructions (DNA). Plant cells also have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole.

Step 2, Observe cells safely. Use a light microscope and a prepared slide of onion skin or cheek cells. Use a 10x eyepiece and a 40x objective: total magnification is 10 x 40 = 400 times. Safety: carry the microscope with two hands, never use the mirror to face the sun, and handle slides and stains with care.

Step 3, Compare animal and plant cells in a table with columns Part, Animal cell, Plant cell, Job. Membrane: yes, yes, controls entry. Nucleus: yes, yes, control centre. Cell wall: no, yes, support. Chloroplast: no, yes, makes food. Add vacuole and cytoplasm rows.

Step 4, Describe sexual reproduction in animals. A male sex cell (sperm) joins a female sex cell (egg) in fertilisation, forming a zygote. Each human sex cell has 23 chromosomes, so the zygote has 23 + 23 = 46, the normal number in body cells. Fish fertilise eggs outside the body, and mammals inside.

Step 5, Describe growth and asexual reproduction. A zygote divides by mitosis: 1 cell, then 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, doubling each time, so after 5 divisions there are 2 to the power 5 = 32 cells. Hydra reproduces asexually by budding, and amoeba splits in two, so offspring are identical.

Step 6, Your turn: calculate the magnification using a 10x eyepiece and a 100x objective, and say how many cells there are after 6 divisions from one cell. Answer: 1000 times; 2 to the power 6 = 64 cells.
